prompt: A channel has 1 MHz of bandwidth and a signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB. What is its Shannon capacity? Assume the band-limited AWGN model with SNR expressed as a power ratio.

options.explanation: This uses the dB number directly as the power ratio, as if the signal were 20 times the noise. Convert first: 20 dB is a power ratio of 100, not 20.
Correct. 20 dB is a power ratio of 100, and 1 MHz times about 6.66 bits per second per hertz is about 6.7 Mbit/s.

That is the ideal zero-ISI real-baseband rate with only two signal levels. The stated AWGN capacity permits optimised signalling and coding under an average-power constraint; it is not a count of a fixed constellation’s levels.
This multiplies bandwidth by S/N directly. Shannon's formula uses the logarithm of one plus the power ratio, which grows much more slowly.

workedExample:
Convert decibels to a power ratio first, then apply Shannon's formula:

```formula
S / N = 10^(SNR_dB / 10)
S / N = 10^(20 / 10) = 100
C = B log_2(1 + S / N)
C = 10⁶ Hz × log_2(101)
C ≈ 10⁶ × 6.66 bit/s ≈ 6.7 Mbit/s
where
S: the average signal power
N: the average noise power; only the ratio S / N matters
SNR_dB: the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels (dB), 20 here
C: the Shannon capacity, in bits per second (bit/s)
B: the channel bandwidth, 1 MHz = 10⁶ hertz (Hz)
log_2: the base-2 logarithm; log_2(101) ≈ 6.66, between 6 (2⁶ = 64) and 7 (2⁷ = 128)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
bit: one binary digit
s: seconds
Mbit/s: megabits per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a signal 100 times stronger than the noise allows about 6.66 bits per second for each hertz, so 1 MHz gives about **6.7 Mbit/s**.
```

This is the capacity of the specified AWGN model; sufficiently long coding can approach it with arbitrarily small error probability.

prompt: A Wi-Fi link uses a 20 MHz channel at 30 dB SNR. Per Shannon, which change raises the capacity limit more: doubling the channel width to 40 MHz (assume the SNR stays at 30 dB), or doubling the signal power (+3 dB SNR) on the 20 MHz channel? Use a single flat AWGN channel, with no additional spatial streams.

options.text: Doubling the power: capacity roughly doubles, because S/N doubles
options.explanation: Capacity grows only with the logarithm of the signal-to-noise ratio, so doubling that ratio adds only about one bit per second per hertz: about 199 → 219 Mbit/s.

options.text: Doubling the width: capacity roughly doubles, from about 199 to about 399 Mbit/s
options.explanation: Correct. Capacity is proportional to bandwidth but only logarithmic in the signal-to-noise ratio. At high SNR, bandwidth is the more effective lever.

options.text: They have the same effect, since both are a factor of two
options.explanation: They enter the formula differently: bandwidth multiplies capacity directly, while the signal-to-noise ratio sits inside a logarithm.

options.text: Neither; capacity is fixed by the modulation scheme
options.explanation: Shannon's limit is independent of modulation. Modulation determines how close you get to the limit, not the limit itself.

workedExample:
At 30 dB the signal is 1000 times the noise; adding approximately 3 dB doubles that to 2000. Apply Shannon's formula to each case:

```formula
C = B log_2(1 + S / N)
C_base ≈ 20 × 10⁶ Hz × 9.97 ≈ 199 Mbit/s
C_2B ≈ 40 × 10⁶ Hz × 9.97 ≈ 399 Mbit/s
C_3dB ≈ 20 × 10⁶ Hz × 10.97 ≈ 219 Mbit/s
where
C: the Shannon capacity, in bits per second
B: the channel bandwidth, in hertz (Hz)
S: the average signal power
N: the average noise power
log_2: the base-2 logarithm; log_2(1001) ≈ 9.97 and log_2(2001) ≈ 10.97
C_base: capacity of the 20 MHz channel at 30 dB
C_2B: capacity with the width doubled to 40 MHz, still at 30 dB
C_3dB: capacity on 20 MHz with S / N doubled (33 dB)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
Mbit/s: megabits per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: doubling the bandwidth doubles capacity (199 to 399 Mbit/s), while doubling the signal power adds only about one bit per second per hertz (199 to 219 Mbit/s).
```

Under the stated constant-SNR assumption, doubling bandwidth doubles capacity. If total signal power instead stays fixed and noise spectral density is constant, doubling bandwidth doubles noise power and reduces SNR by approximately 3 dB. Actual Wi-Fi throughput also includes coding, contention, pilots and protocol overhead.
